passage: In the Gurugram architecture office, Suraj spread Sahil's drawings across the table. "The facade is strong. But the stair layout doesn't meet the fire rules. You'll need to redo it." Sahil felt a flicker of heat in his neck. Then he breathed. "You're right. I missed the second exit. That's my mistake." He made a note. "I'm good at facades, not great at the rules yet. Could I sit with Meenal for an hour? She knows them cold." Suraj nodded. "Good idea." Walking back to his desk, Sahil didn't replay the meeting or plan a comeback. He opened the file and started on the stair. At six he left, the stair half-done and the facade still something he was proud of.

qa.q: What did Sahil miss in the stair layout?
qa.a: He missed the second exit.

qa.q: What did Sahil feel when Suraj pointed out the mistake, and how did he handle it?
qa.a: He felt a flicker of heat in his neck, a moment of embarrassment, but he breathed and stayed calm.

qa.q: What choice did Sahil make after the feedback, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He admitted the mistake, named his strength and his gap, and asked to learn from Meenal, which turned feedback into a plan.

qa.q: How might Suraj see Sahil after this meeting?
qa.a: Suraj probably sees Sahil as someone who can take honest feedback without drama, which builds trust.

grounding: A young architect accepts his strengths and flaws, takes a correction calmly and admits a mistake while still feeling worthy.

passage:
"Rukmini, your piece on the flower market was lovely. But you got the vendor's name wrong. He's already called twice."
Rukmini winced, then pulled her notebook closer. "Oh no. Which name?"
"You wrote Gopal. It's Govind."
"That's on me. I copied it from my notes too fast. I'll call him and apologise, and we'll run a correction tomorrow."
"You're taking this well."
"It stings. But one wrong name doesn't make the whole piece bad. The opening's still good, isn't it?"
Divyansh grinned. "The opening's the best thing you've written."
"Then I'll keep that and fix the name. And from now on I'll read names back to people."
"Want me to sit with you while you call?"
"No, I've got it. Thanks, though."

qa.q: What name did Rukmini write for the vendor?
qa.a: She wrote Gopal, but it's Govind.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel about the mistake, and what shows it?
qa.a: It stung, as she says, but she stayed steady, knowing one wrong name doesn't make the whole piece bad.

qa.q: What did Rukmini choose to do about the mistake?
qa.a: She owned it, planned to call and apologise, ran a correction and decided to read names back to people.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel working with someone who takes feedback like this?
qa.a: Divyansh probably feels relieved and respectful, since honest feedback doesn't make her collapse.

grounding: A young journalist takes a correction calmly, admits the mistake and fixes it while still valuing what she did well.

passage: Last month I sent a client the wrong version of the budget sheet. Baljeet, my team lead, called me in, and I could feel the old instinct: defend myself or crumble. I did neither. I said, "That was my error. I didn't check the file name before sending. I'll call the client today and set up a two-step check." Baljeet nodded, then added that my presentations were rushed too. That stung. I asked for one example, took notes, and slept fine that night. I'm Ujjwal, twenty-five, and I'm not the best on the team. I'm good at client calls and bad at slides. Both things are true, and neither makes me worth less as a person.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal send the client by mistake?
qa.a: The wrong version of the budget sheet.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Baljeet mentioned rushed presentations?
qa.a: It stung, but Ujjwal stayed calm, asking for an example and sleeping fine that night.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal's response to the mistake get right?
qa.a: Ujjwal owned the error plainly, fixed it with the client and set up a check, without defending or collapsing.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Ujjwal after this meeting?
qa.a: Baljeet likely sees someone dependable who can hear feedback and act on it.

grounding: Shows a young professional who admits a mistake and takes feedback calmly, holding strengths and flaws together.

passage:
Observation note, Class 3 teacher review. I watched Pallavi's maths lesson on Tuesday. The fractions activity fell flat; half the class was lost by the ten-minute mark. Afterwards I gave her my notes. She read them, winced once, and said, "You're right. I rushed the pizza example." Then she asked what I had liked. I told her: her calm voice, and that she knows every child's name. She wrote both lists down, side by side, without arguing or over-apologising. On Thursday she retaught the lesson with paper strips. It worked. Next step: I have asked her to show the paper-strip idea to the new teachers.
Rajni

qa.q: What did Pallavi use when she retaught the lesson?
qa.a: Paper strips.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's single wince suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: The feedback stung a little, but she felt secure enough to accept it without collapsing.

qa.q: What did Pallavi's way of taking feedback do well?
qa.a: She agreed with the fair point, asked for strengths too and wrote both lists side by side, then acted on it.

qa.q: How does Rajni see Pallavi after the review?
qa.a: Rajni sees a teacher worth trusting, which is why Pallavi is asked to share the idea with new teachers.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional who takes critical feedback calmly, holds strengths and flaws together and improves.

passage:
Thursday. Lakshmi reviewed my code today and left fourteen comments. Fourteen! A year ago I'd have gone to the washroom and cried, or argued every one. Today I read them with chai. Nine were right, three were style things I can live with, and two I disagreed with, so I said so, politely, with reasons. She agreed on one. I also admitted I'd missed a bug that crashed the test server on Monday. Nobody died. I'm not a genius. I'm also not a fraud. I'm someone who writes decent code and is still learning to write tests. Somehow that feels steady, like standing on flat ground.
Sonali

qa.q: How many comments did Lakshmi leave?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: How does Sonali feel about the review now, compared with a year ago?
qa.a: Sonali feels calm and steady, where a year ago the same comments would have brought tears or arguments.

qa.q: What does Sonali do that shows steady self-respect?
qa.a: Sorting the comments fairly, disagreeing politely with reasons and openly admitting the missed bug.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see Sonali's polite disagreement?
qa.a: Lakshmi seems to respect it, since she agreed with one of the two points.

grounding: Shows a young professional who takes feedback without collapse, admits a mistake and feels worthy while still learning.
